    "answerable": [
      "Column-scale water balance closure: P = ET + total runoff + drainage + dStorage",

      "Seasonal and snow-driven controls on partitioning (snowmelt timing, dry-season ET)",

      "Return-flow and inter-column groundwater redistribution effects on runoff"

Five columns sample the dominant precipitation/land-cover/soil regimes (high montane forest, mid-elevation mixed conifer, transitional shrub-forest, valley grassland/agriculture, and a lee-side dry slope), enough to bracket the partitioning gradient and align with available SNOTEL and flux/ET validation sites without excessive redundancy.",

  "elm_config": {
    "DATM_CLMNCEP_YR_START": "1980",
    "DATM_CLMNCEP_YR_END": "2014",

    "Single-column (single-point) ELM configuration at 5 sites",
    "Atmospheric forcing (GSWP3 v1 or site-corrected reanalysis) with orographic precipitation representation",
    "Surface dataset with site-appropriate PFT and soil texture from gridded databases",
    "ELM BGC/SP hydrology with variably saturated soil column and groundwater/drainage scheme (QCHARGE, ZWT diagnostics)",

feasibility.verdict: Partially feasible: precipitation partitioning into ET, total runoff, and deep drainage (recharge proxy) is directly diagnosable in single-column ELM; full watershed-integrated streamflow validation is limited because single columns do not perform lateral routing.
answerable: Column-scale water balance closure: P = ET + total runoff + drainage + dStorage
Fractional partitioning of precipitation into ET, surface+subsurface runoff, and bottom drainage (recharge proxy) across an elevation/land-cover gradient
Seasonal and snow-driven controls on partitioning (snowmelt timing, dry-season ET)
Point/pixel validation of ET against flux-tower and remote-sensing ET products
Validation of snowpack (SWE) against SNOTEL stations for melt-driven runoff timing
not_answerable: Gauge-comparable streamflow hydrograph at the HUC8 outlet (requires lateral/river routing, e.g., MOSART, not single-column ELM)
Spatially continuous recharge maps or groundwater head validation (needs distributed subsurface model / PFLOTRAN coupling)
Return-flow and inter-column groundwater redistribution effects on runoff

parsed.n_justification: The Naches sub-watershed spans a strong orographic gradient from high Cascade forests (>1800 m, snow-dominated) to the semi-arid lower valley (~450 m). Five columns sample the dominant precipitation/land-cover/soil regimes (high montane forest, mid-elevation mixed conifer, transitional shrub-forest, valley grassland/agriculture, and a lee-side dry slope), enough to bracket the partitioning gradient and align with available SNOTEL and flux/ET validation sites without excessive redundancy.
requires_capabilities: Atmospheric forcing (GSWP3 v1 or site-corrected reanalysis) with orographic precipitation representation
Surface dataset with site-appropriate PFT and soil texture from gridded databases
ELM BGC/SP hydrology with variably saturated soil column and groundwater/drainage scheme (QCHARGE, ZWT diagnostics)
SNOTEL SWE observations for snowpack validation (e.g., Bumping Lake, Morse Lake)
Flux-tower and/or remote-sensing ET products (AmeriFlux, MODIS MOD16, OpenET) for ET validation
USGS streamflow at Naches gauges for context (not direct single-column validation; would require MOSART routing for gauge comparison)
assumptions: Recharge is approximated by simulated bottom-boundary drainage/groundwater recharge flux (QDRAI/QCHARGE); no explicit deep aquifer or PFLOTRAN coupling in the base run
Each column is representative of its elevation/land-cover band; sub-grid heterogeneity within a band is neglected
First 5 years (1980-1984) treated as spin-up/adjustment; partitioning analysis uses 1985-2014
Water-balance partitioning is reported as area-weighted column fractions, not a routed basin hydrograph
Irrigation and water withdrawals in the valley agricultural column are not represented unless an irrigation module is enabled; valley ET may be underestimated
Precipitation forcing captures orographic gradient adequately after site elevation lapse-rate correction
